catalog_citation: Blust, Robert. 1988. Sketches of the morphology and phonology of Bornean languages 2: Mukah (Melanau). In H. Steinhauer (ed.), Papers in Western Austronesian Linguistics No. 3, 151-216. Pacific Linguistics A-78. Canberra: ANU.
catalog_locator: sec. 2.5.1 Phonological rules, rule 1 (stress placement), pp. 178-179
catalog_quote: 1 (stress placement) As stress placement in Mukah citation forms is apparently governed by a rather complex set of conditions, it will perhaps be clearest if the general case (a) is stated first, followed by each subcase (b-d) in descending order of importance: (a) the penultimate vowel of a word receives stress. ... (b) if the penultimate vowel of a word is schwa, stress shifts to the final syllable. ... (c) following /a/ and preceding word boundary high vowels receive stress (and perhaps added length - not mentioned further). This subpart of the stress rule is posited to account for the fact that minimal pairs such as ... differ not only in number of syllables, but also in placement of stress. The shift of stress in such cases may be motivated by a desire to avoid homophony, or may have been a product of unnatural emphasis for my sake. ... In a sequence of like vowels the first vowel …

new_statements.quote: 2.23 Suprasegmental Phonemes are predictable at the level of the phonological word. Spoken in isolation, a word has primary stress on the final syllable nucleus, accompanied by a rise in pitch which falls off from a peak to approximately the starting datum level. Polysyllabic words have a secondary stress, accompanied by a less marked pitch change, on the penultimate syllable nucleus. [p.50] ... /'/ primary stress, a toneme of loudness of the syllable nucleus, occurs on final syllable of stressed words in syntagms, and of words spoken in isolation [p.51] ... Footnote 1: This general rule is perturbed when the penultimate vowel is /a/, before a final /ə/. Then both the last two syllables have approximately equal stress, at level /"/ [p.51]

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Clayre 1972: the 94.3 MB PDF the reader symlinked was pruned by the LING corpus cleanup at (symlink now dangles; >80 MB so not refetched); verified against the surviving text layer (lines 2467-2533) and.. Sec. 2.23 (printed p.50): 'Supraselemental [scanned for Suprasegmental] Phonemes are predictable at the level of the phonological word. Spoken in isolation, a word has primary stress on the final syllable nucleus, accompanied by a rise in pitch which falls off from a peak to approximately the starting datum level. Polysyllabic words have a secondary stress, accompanied by a less marked pitch change, on the penultimate syllable nucleus.' Sec. 2.231 Stress (printed p.51): '/'/ primary stress…
new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Mukah Melanau has an empty rule and no existing statements; Clayre supplies the placement (predictable final primary stress, penult secondary). The description is founded on the Dalat dialect of the Central Melanau dialect group (thesis abstract p.5/line 183: 'a description of the Dalat dialect'), with Mukah cited as a neighbouring dialect in 2.4; Clayre calls final stress 'the typical Melanau stress placement' (p.57 fn.1) and section 2.4 Dialect variation records no stress differences among dialects. download note: era.ed.ac.uk and hdl.handle.net gave automated download rc=52 by automated download; the the Internet Archive landing page resolved but the bitstream is 9…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-phonemic and predictable: primary stress (with a pitch rise-fall) falls on the final syllable nucleus of the word, in isolation and in phrases; p.36 adds that it 'falls predictably on the final syllable and is therefore not emically relevant'; p.57 notes final stress holds even in Malay cognates ([ka'in] 'cloth' vs Malay ['kain]).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Polysyllabic words carry a secondary stress, with a less marked pitch change, on the penultimate syllable nucleus (sec. 2.23 p.50; /"/ in 2.231 p.51).
new_statements.exceptions: Footnote 1 p.51: when the penult vowel is /a/ and the final vowel is /ə/, the last two syllables have approximately equal stress at secondary level (e.g. /takadəŋ/ 'stagnant water'). Also p.50: final vowel vs final semivowel words differ etically in where the predictable final-nucleus stress lands ([ba'u:] /bau/ 'Bau' vs ['bau] /baw/ 'up').
new_statements.identity_note: Clayre 1972 describes the Dalat dialect of Melanau (Central dialect group, ISO mel / cent2101), 'amplified by reference to the other known dialects' including neighbouring Mukah; the stress statement is given for Dalat and characterised as typical of Melanau generally, with no dialectal stress differences reported in his dialect-variation section (2.4).

readall_conflicts: held by the project already: Blust 1988 (Mukah) gives penultimate stress shifting to the final syllable when the penult is schwa (catalog 'weight-hedged'), while Clayre 1972 describes the Dalat dialect with primary stress on the final syllable and secondary on the penult; that standing Mukah-vs-Dalat difference is untouched here. The unobtained Chou 1999 thesis is, per Glottolog, based on Clayre 1972 (Dalat), so it is unlikely to add independent evidence on Mukah.

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) The deciding quotation is verbatim in the Blust 1988 text we hold at sec. 2.5.1 rule 1, pp. 178-179, with matching examples. (2) The source is a first-hand phonology/morphology sketch by Blust in Pacific Linguistics -- the only phonological description of the Mukah dialect; Glottolog's only larger work (Clayre 1972) is on the Dalat dialect. Web search found no instrumental or later prosodic study of Melanau; the 2016 Malaysian phonology article on Mukah (downloaded) treats segments only. Blust 2013 (held) and Smith 2023 (downloaded) both restate penultimate stress with final stress after a schwa penult, consistent with the 'weight-hedged, full-vs-reduced-vowel, right edge' coding; the hedging in our record mirrors Blust's own ('apparently', 'may have been a product of unnatural emphasis for my sake') and is appropriate. (3) list of works to obtain is short: Clayre 1972 (open at Edinburgh ERA but unreachable

sources.quote: 'Identical patterns are found in other Western Indonesian languages in Borneo, including In Mukah Melanau where Blust (1988: 178) notes that stress occurs typically on the penultimate syllable in phrasal contexts but that stress occurs on the final syllable if the penultimate syllable has a schwa nucleus.' (secondary, cites our deciding source; note Blust actually says 'citation forms', not 'phrasal contexts')
sources.locator: offprint p. [14] (section on Western Indonesian stress shift)
sources.note: Recent comparative treatment that restates the Mukah Melanau rule (penultimate; final after schwa penult) from Blust 1988:178 and frames schwa as weightless -- supports the weight (full-vs-reduced-vowel) reading of our 'weight-hedged' coding; usable as a corroborating secondary citation.
